question.text:
Find the solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\!A\mathbf{x}=W\mathbf{b},$ where

\[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad W = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\!A\mathbf{x}=W\mathbf{b},$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\!A)^T{:}$

\begin{align*} (W\!A)^T \cdot W\!A \mathbf{x} &= (W\!A)^T \cdot W\mathbf{b} \\[5pt] A^T (W^T W) A \mathbf{x} &= A^T (W^T W)\mathbf{b} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Now, since

\[ W^T W = \begin{bmatrix} 2^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1^2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

our normal equation can be written as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & -4 \\ 4 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 8 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 12 & -6 \\ -6 & 5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 14 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 12 & -6 \\ -6 & 5 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 14 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{12\cdot5 - (-6) \cdot (-6)} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 6 \\ 6 & 12 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 14 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{24} \begin{bmatrix} 40 \\ 24 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{5}{3} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad W = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $\mathbf{b}$ above. If the normal equation for the corresponding weighted least-squares problem $W\!A \mathbf{x} = W\mathbf{b}$ is given by

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{a} & -27 \\-27 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{b} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{c} \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} \]

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
question.explanation:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\!A\mathbf{x}=W\mathbf{b},$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\!A)^T{:}$

\begin{align*} (W\!A)^T \cdot W\!A \mathbf{x} &= (W\!A)^T \cdot W\mathbf{b} \\[5pt] A^T (W^T W) A \mathbf{x} &= A^T (W^T W)\mathbf{b} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Now, since

\[ W^T W = \begin{bmatrix} 2^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1^2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

our normal equation can be written as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 12 & -4 \\ 6 & -2 \\-3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{81} & -27 \\ -27 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{9} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{12} \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\[ a+b+c=81+9+12 = 102. \]

question.text:
\[ A=\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 3 \\ 4 & -6 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad W = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $\mathbf{b}$ above. If the normal equation for the corresponding weighted least-squares problem $W\!A \mathbf{x} = W\mathbf{b}$ is given by

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{a} & -42 \\ -42 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{b} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{c} \\ 36 \end{bmatrix} \]

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
question.explanation:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\!A\mathbf{x}=W\mathbf{b},$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\!A)^T{:}$

\begin{align*} (W\!A)^T \cdot W\!A \mathbf{x} &= (W\!A)^T \cdot W\mathbf{b} \\[5pt] A^T (W^T W) A \mathbf{x} &= A^T (W^T W)\mathbf{b} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Now, since

\[ W^T W = \begin{bmatrix} 2^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1^2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

our normal equation can be written as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 4 & 2 \\ 3 & -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 3 \\ 4 & -6 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 4 & 2 \\ 3 & -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 4 & 2 \\ 3 & -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -8 & 12 \\ 4 & -6 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} -8 & 4 & 2 \\ 12 & -6 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{36} & -42 \\ -42 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{81} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{-16} \\ 36 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\[ a+b+c=36+81+(-16) = 101. \]

question.text:
Find the solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\!A\mathbf{x}=W\mathbf{b},$ where

\[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad W = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\!A\mathbf{x}=W\mathbf{b},$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\!A)^T{:}$

\begin{align*} (W\!A)^T \cdot W\!A \mathbf{x} &= (W\!A)^T \cdot W\mathbf{b} \\[5pt] A^T (W^T W) A \mathbf{x} &= A^T (W^T W)\mathbf{b} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Now, since

\[ W^T W = \begin{bmatrix} 1^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1^2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

our normal equation can be written as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 14 & 9 \\ 9 & 9 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 14 & 9 \\ 9 & 9 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{14\cdot 9 - 9 \cdot 9} \begin{bmatrix} 9 & -9 \\ -9 & 14 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{45} \begin{bmatrix} 45\\ -45\end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad W = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $\mathbf{b}$ above. If the normal equation for the corresponding weighted least-squares problem $W\!A \mathbf{x} = W\mathbf{b}$ is given by

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{a} & -15 \\-15 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{b} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -19 \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{c} \end{bmatrix} \]

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
question.explanation:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\!A\mathbf{x}=W\mathbf{b},$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\!A)^T{:}$

\begin{align*} (W\!A)^T \cdot W\!A \mathbf{x} &= (W\!A)^T \cdot W\mathbf{b} \\[5pt] A^T (W^T W) A \mathbf{x} &= A^T (W^T W)\mathbf{b} \\[5pt] \end{align*}

Now, since

\[ W^T W = \begin{bmatrix} 1^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1^2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

our normal equation can be written as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ -9 & 9 \\ 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &=\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 18 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{22} & -15 \\ -15 & \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{13} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} -19 \\ \bbox[lightgray,2pt]{24} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Therefore, we have

\[ a+b+c=22+13+24 = 59. \]
